The Olds Calais Was An Indy 500 Pace Car Edition With No Pace

TB
By Tyler Brooks Viral Concepts & Prototype Lead • via Carscoops Wire
⚡ Visual Story
Source & Photography: Carscoops Wire Dispatch Verified Editorial Asset
⚡ Executive Takeaways & Key Highlights

  • But it took until 1953 — 42 years after the inaugural race — for automakers to realize they could make bank by peddling replicas of the sedans, coupes and convertibles that led the field.

⚡ EDITORIAL TAKE • TYLER BROOKS Viral Concepts & Prototype Lead

Automotive Innovation & Market Feasibility

Concept prototypes and viral vehicle reveals offer an exciting window into the automotive industry's future design language. Big Picture: Market reception and formal OEM production announcements will determine which concept innovations make it to consumer streets.

For as long as there's been an Indianapolis 500, there's been an Indianapolis 500 pace car. But it took until 1953 — 42 years after the inaugural race — for automakers to realize they could make bank by peddling replicas of the sedans, coupes and convertibles that led the field. Some of these lookalikes, cars like the orange and white 1969 Chevy Camaro SS/RS, and the the black and silver 1978 Corvette pace car replica , are blue-chip collector classics. Others, like this Oldsmobile Calais 500 , which is up for auction through Bring a Trailer, are rarely remembered.

📌 The Core Development

Oldsmobile reportedly built 2,998 Calais 500 commemorative pace car editions (confusingly, some sources say just 242), though none of them looked anything like the real version. The genuine Indy Calais driven by Rockford Files star James Garner, (there were actually two cars) was a special convertible version that Olds never offered to the public.

Also not available via your Oldsmobile dealer, was the real pace car's specially tuned 2.7-liter version of GM's 2.5-liter Tech-4 inline-4 that whipped up 215 horsepower to ensure it could stay ahead of the open-wheel Indy racers.

🔍 Background & Sector Context

The Calais was new for 1985, and shared its front-wheel drive N-body platform with the Pontiac Grand Am and Buick Somerset Regal. It came with either two or four doors, both with a vertical back window style lifted from Olds' bigger cars, a hangover from the 1970s that looked about as modern as cycle fenders and wooden spoked wheels.

All pace car editions got the two-door body, and came dressed in red metallic paint with a silver lower body, silver pace car graphics plastered across the doors, plus another sticker on the tail, and a couple of badges. They also got a silver and red bucket seat interior that made the car look like it was built to celebrate a NASA launch, not an automobile race. And, after that, Oldsmobile seems to have run out of ideas.

📊 Industry & Real-World Impact

There were no mechanical upgrades, and you could even order your Calais 500 pace car edition with that year's standard Calais engine, the 92-horsepower 2.5-liter inline-4. Maybe the 500 referred to its 0-60 mph time. Salvation of sorts came in the form of an optional 3.0-liter V6, which pushed out 125 hp, though that meant forgoing a five-speed manual option, and putting up with a three-speed automatic.

🔮 Strategic Outlook & What Lies Ahead

Motorweek took a Calais V6 from zero to 60 mph in 11.4 seconds, performance it described as "commendable." Which just shows how easily pleased reviewers were back then, after having endured a decade of cars with smog-choked motors.

This auction Calais 500 is one of what the owner claims were 600 cars ordered with the 3.0-liter V6, and shows just 13,000 miles. Its silver interior looks virtually untouched, and the exterior is pretty peachy, too. Only the grubby engine and deteriorated hood insulation lets the the look down. Our favorite detail besides that upholstery has to be the Auto-Calculator trip computer, which must have seemed incredibly trick back in 1985.
